summary.one_line: Home vegetable gardeners pay small amounts for printable planners and larger amounts for planning software; free date calculators are everywhere, so the opening is a personal frost-date planting calendar joined to a printable season planner, sold at about $15 before the January to March planning window.

go_hold.subject: Garden Planner as the candidate fourth business (blueprint only, no launch)
go_hold.rationale: Highest adjusted score in Scout run 2026-11-scout-01 and the only candidate with VERIFIED demand and price evidence that passes every gate. The changes: the free calculator must be the traffic engine, and the paid kit must do what free tools do not (a personal, printable season plan from one frost date).
go_hold.falsifying_test: If the free planting-calendar pages get 500+ organic or Pinterest sessions between 2027-01-01 and 2027-03-15 and the kit sells nothing, hold the niche. Owner-adjustable rule, not a forecast.

key_findings.statement: Paid printable garden planners on Etsy show real purchase activity: 27 item reviews (MissMikesPlace, $7.05, shop 1.1k sales), 26 item reviews (MeadowGates, shop 2.2k sales) and 3 item reviews at $18.00 (ReformStead, shop 1.8k sales).
key_findings.notes: Review counts are a lower bound on sales; shop sales cover all of each shop's products.

key_findings.statement: Printable garden planners sell at $3.99 (8-page grid), $7.05 (35 pages) and $18.00 (200+ pages).
Garden-planning software charges $50 a year or $85 for two years (Almanac Garden Planner, 7-day trial) and $7 or $14 a month billed yearly (Seedtime paid plans).

Free planting-date tools exist: Seedtime's calendar is free forever with suggested seeding, transplant and harvest dates; Johnny's calculator takes a frost-free date and returns indoor-start and set-out windows; Vital Seeds gives away a planning spreadsheet.
41% of US households (about 53.7 million) did some food gardening in 2021, spending an average of $88.24 on it (National Gardening Association survey, as reported in April 2022).
key_findings.notes: 2021 data, a pandemic-era high (33.1% in 2019). Newer NGA editions are paid and were not read.

key_findings.statement: USDA's 2023 hardiness map moved about half the country into the next warmer half zone, so many gardeners' existing planting dates are out of date.
key_findings.notes: The 'out of date' part is an inference.

key_findings.statement: Frost dates can come from NOAA NCEI's 1991-2020 U.S. Climate Normals, which Data.gov lists under CC0 (public domain). The annual normals include last-spring and first-fall 32F, 28F and 36F probability dates at 10-90%, for 7,300+ stations with temperature normals. Climate.gov's last-freeze map uses the 50% date.
key_findings.notes: Element names ANN-TMIN-PRBLST-T32FP50 (spring) and ANN-TMIN-PRBFST-T32FP50 (fall). Not yet checked: the date encoding in the CSV, and the coverage of the freeze elements, which is a subset of the 7,300.
